S01.basis: The plateau geology file (07) gives no flux for any seep or spring, so a required flux has nothing to be set against at any cycle time: its one analogue is a concentration, read from an abstract, at which one batch is the sulfide in 5.3 million m3 of cave air (60 ppmv in active sulfuric-acid caves). One full batch needs 13319 mol of hydrogen sulfide, 454 kg, a mole for each mole of sulfur dioxide in the King's Chamber, which is 0.15 mol/s and 166 t a year at one batch every 24 h, and 0.00041 to 3.8 mol/s over the cycle times taken; the hypothesis states no cycle rate either, so the required flux is itself undefined (07 section 4.4).

S19.basis: With the Gallery half full and a cycle of 24 h (the hypothesis states none; 1 h to 1 yr is taken as its range), 87 percent of the sulfur dioxide crosses the level surface into the water (0.1 to 97 percent over the ranges of the inputs), which over those ranges is neither always at the 90 percent from which the criterion passes the claim nor always under the 50 percent below which it fails it. The water could hold 98 percent at equilibrium, so the rate decides. It depends on the cycle time, on whether the gas over the water stands still or convects (gas-side coefficient 0.003 to 10 mm/s, assumed) and on the film on the water's side of the surface (liquid-film coefficient 0.001 to 0.01 mm/s, assumed with no source), none of which the hypothesis gives; the 87 percent is for a gas-side coefficient of 1.5 mm/s and a liquid-film coefficient of 0.01 mm/s. At those two coefficients the share passes 50 percent after 7.8 h and passes 90 percent after 28 h, with a time constant of 10.7 h toward the 96.9 percent that the water holds by Henry's law alone, without the dissociation counted in the 98 percent; in a cycle of 24 h it runs from 2 to 94 percent over the ranges of the other inputs, the two coefficients among them, so stating a cycle of that length would not settle the claim without them. The model gives the gas the whole cycle over the half-full Gallery, though it stands over the water only until the water has risen (S18): in a contact of the 1 h that the ledger carries for one fill, a time the hypothesis does not state either, the share is 9 percent (0.014 to 94 percent over fills of 10 minutes to 24 h and the ranges of the other inputs).

S22.basis: Emptying the whole Gallery draws 573 m3 of gas into it and the King's Chamber holds 320 m3, so at least 44 percent of the gas over the water is outside air, come down the shafts of S14 or in through the masonry joints (39 percent at the least). Its nitrogen hardly dissolves: if all the sulfur dioxide dissolved, the oxidation used every mole of oxygen it could and the water arrived free of dissolved gas, the rising water would still push 33 percent of the gas back (29 to 37 percent over the ranges of the inputs), and 54 percent of a mixture that carries the oxygen for all its sulfur. Nothing is pushed back only if air is under 2.0 percent of the gas (2.4 percent at most), which brings oxygen for 0.8 percent of the sulfur, while S14 to S17 carry air into the Gallery; the hypothesis states no gas fraction, and the whole Gallery is taken as emptied because S18 raises the water again in the four activations with which S12 fills it. Taking the least air that emptying the whole Gallery admits, not a gas without air, as the end most favourable to the hypothesis is a judgement call.

S23.basis: Fresh water lets bare limestone neutralise 41 percent of the strongest batch before gypsum can form (Tier 0), and the layer that then grows by acid diffusing through it reaches 3.7 micrometres in a cycle of 24 h (the hypothesis states none; 1 h to 1 yr is taken as its range) (0.1 to 74 micrometres over the ranges of the inputs). One fill of fresh water can dissolve 0.63 mm of gypsum, 173 times that layer (7.7 times at the least); even the most gypsum a whole batch can lay down is 55 percent of what one fill dissolves (76 percent at most), so a fill that comes to saturation strips it; every cycle then starts on bare stone, which loses up to 0.21 mm per cycle and 2.1 mm in ten in bringing each batch to saturation (1.6 to 4.9 mm over the ranges of the inputs). A fill that stands still strips the layer a bare wall grows in one cycle by diffusion alone only if it stands at least 0.1 times as long as the acid stood (0.19 times at most). The hypothesis does not state that time; over the range taken, 1.9e-05 to 1 of the acid's, a still fill dissolves 0.0099 to 23 times that layer, and 0.65 times at the 0.042 the ledger takes as its value. The acid of the next batch does not strip it: still acid dissolves it from outside while it grows from beneath and leaves at most 49 percent of it (7 to 61 percent), about 26 percent once the batch's bisulfate is counted (4 to 35 percent). So whether the layer lasts depends on how long the fresh water stands against the wall and on how it moves, neither of which the hypothesis states.
